title: One Bias After Another: Mechanistic Reward Shaping and Persistent Biases in Language Reward Models
claim: Reward models show opposing length biases across architectures, and a lightweight post-hoc correction closes the gap without hurting accuracy.
layout: 1 panel, grouped bars per model, original vs debiased hatched, error bars
description: A single wide grouped bar chart of accuracy (%) on the y-axis (0–100) for five reward models on the x-axis: DeBERTa, Skywork-Qwen0.6B, Skywork-Qwen8B, AllenAI and Skywork-Llama. A vertical divider separates DeBERTa from the others. Each model has four bars with error bars. Orange is concise-correct and green is verbose-correct. Solid bars are the normal model and hatched bars are the debiased model. A legend runs along the top. DeBERTa's solid green bar is far above its orange bar, which shows a verbosity bias. The other models show the reverse, with green lower than orange. After debiasing, the orange and green bars sit much closer together. The eye goes first to DeBERTa's tall green bar, then to the shrinking green-orange gaps in the hatched bars.
caption: RM accuracy selecting correct over incorrect answers on GSM8K with bootstrapped 95% CI. An unbiased RM should show no gap between concise and verbose performance. DeBERTa rewards verbosity (green bar higher) while state-of-the-art models can overcorrect and penalize it (green bar lower). Mechanistic correction via probe nulling closes these gaps without degrading baseline accuracy.
abstract: Reward Models (RMs) are crucial for online alignment of language models (LMs) with human preferences. However, RM-based preference-tuning is vulnerable to reward hacking, whereby LM policies learn undesirable behaviors from flawed RMs. By systematically measuring biases in five high-quality RMs, including the state-of-the-art, we find that issues persist despite prior work with respect to length, sycophancy, and overconfidence. We also discover new issues related to bias toward model-specific ``styles'' and answer-order. We categorize RM failures as tractable or resistant to linear intervention and propose a simple post-hoc intervention to mitigate low-complexity biases that arise from spurious correlations. Our proposed mechanistic reward shaping reduces targeted biases without degrading reward quality and while using minimal labeled data. The method is extensible to new biases, model-internal, and generalizes out-of-distribution.
